cards.title: Sizing the SMS channel for your store
cards.summary: SMS is an owned retention channel; source argues it should account for at least 5–15% of brand total sales and cites client SMS bills under $1,000/month producing tens of thousands monthly.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch or resource an SMS channel, or benchmarking whether your current SMS program is underperforming relative to the channel's potential.
steps: Treat SMS as an owned retention channel like email: the list is not subject to ad auctions or algorithm changes, so revenue compounds month over month once built.

Judge the channel on its sales-share contribution. The source's benchmark: done correctly, SMS should account for at least 5–15% of total brand sales. Treat this as the presenter's agency heuristic, not a computed industry figure.
Compare channel cost to revenue: the source cites several client accounts spending less than $1,000/month on SMS to generate tens of thousands per month. Case-study result, not a promise.

Check a simple list-size math argument before investing: going from 5,000 to 10,000 subscribers on identical campaigns does not double orders (diminishing returns) — the source's illustrative example is roughly 100 orders becoming 160–180, not 200. Growth still compounds, so not growing caps your ceiling.
Audit which capabilities you already have in email before layering SMS, since most SMS revenue comes from omni-channel flows shared with email.
caveats: 5–15% of sales and the sub-$1,000-bill examples come from the presenter's agency clients; your category, list quality and offer mix will differ.
Diminishing returns are real: more subscribers from unqualified traffic dilutes performance.

cards.title: Choose and configure an SMS platform for Shopify-style ecommerce
cards.summary: Pick Klaviyo, Attentive or Postscript — they all do the same core job — and configure number verification, subscriber import, signup forms, opt-out language, smart sending, quiet hours and keyword responses.
cards.use_when: Setting up an SMS sending account for the first time, or migrating existing SMS subscribers into a platform that also holds your email.
steps: Choose a platform: the source names Klaviyo, Attentive and Postscript and says all three send essentially the same simple texts, so you cannot go badly wrong. It prefers Klaviyo so email and SMS flows live under one flow view rather than splitting email in Klaviyo and SMS in Attentive/Postscript.
In platform settings, start SMS setup, pick your sending country, and verify a toll-free number. Note the source's caution: Canadian numbers can cost two SMS credits instead of one.
Upload your existing SMS subscriber list from CSV or other file so previously collected consent carries over.
Create the signup form — the platform states you need a form to keep collecting SMS subscribers; also keep an email pop-up active.
Set opt-out language to whatever you prefer (e.g. 'unsub') under message add-ons.
In sender preferences, decide on smart sending: when on, a subscriber will not receive more than one SMS campaign within a 24-hour window. Toggle per your cadence.
Leave SMS quiet hours on default — it blocks delivery during the restricted hours rather than sending.
Set keyword responses (e.g. texting JOIN to your number adds the person to the list and can trigger a discount), plus short links and terms. Verify the current interface, since menus change.
caveats: Platform UIs and pricing change; verify current setup screens, credit costs and quiet-hour defaults before relying on this walkthrough.
Country-specific costs and rules differ — the source only demonstrates a US setup.

cards.title: Two-step pop-up to convert email visitors into SMS subscribers
cards.summary: Split email and SMS into separate pop-up steps, lead with your best offer in the email step, and use 'finish signing up with text to activate 20% off' style copy on the SMS step.
cards.use_when: Building or redesigning an onsite pop-up whose goal is to grow an SMS list from traffic you are already paying for.
steps: Do not put many fields on one pop-up. Avoid asking for first name, last name, occupation, location and phone all at once; each extra field is a hurdle that suppresses opt-in.
Make the pop-up two steps: an email step first, then an SMS step. Smaller sequential hurdles convert better than one large ask.

Decide the offer architecture. Many brands offer less for email and a bonus for SMS (e.g. 15% email, extra 5% SMS). The source disagrees: it prefers giving the best offer up front to email, because you get far more email opt-ins, then re-words the SMS step to capture SMS subscribers anyway. Test both if you are unsure.

Use the source's tested SMS step copy: 'finish signing up with text to activate 20% off' — i.e. tell the visitor the SMS step is what activates the discount they already saw, rather than dangling a new incentive.
Time the pop-up. The source's recommended delay is 6 to 10 seconds after page load — enough for the visitor to engage with the page before being interrupted.
Track opt-in rate separately for the email step and the SMS step so you can tell which step is losing people.
caveats: 'Finish signing up with text to activate 20% off' is the source's tested wording across its accounts, not a universal guarantee; validate on your own traffic.
Whether the best offer goes up front or is split between email and SMS is contested — the source presents its preference against the common alternative, not a proven rule.

cards.title: Other SMS list-growth levers beyond the pop-up
cards.summary: The pop-up is the single biggest SMS list driver; the source frames seven growth methods and treats list growth as non-negotiable because an ungrown list caps campaign and flow reach.
cards.use_when: Planning next quarter's SMS subscriber acquisition when pop-up opt-ins alone are not adding enough subscribers.
steps: Make the onsite pop-up your primary method — the source calls it by far the number one way it grows client SMS lists.
Add keyword opt-ins: configure a JOIN-style keyword so people who text it join the list and can claim a discount. Promote the keyword offsite where phone-first audiences are.

Use the flow-generated opt-in surface: your existing SMS flows and signup forms are additional points where consent is captured, so make sure forms are live on the site rather than only in the platform.

Only count qualified buyers as valuable subscribers. The source is explicit that the larger the list of actual buyers, the larger the impact; bought or unqualified numbers add cost and unsubscribes without proportional orders.

Accept diminishing returns in your forecasting: doubling the list does not double orders on identical campaigns, but still increases order volume. Model the channel on incremental lift, not a linear multiple.
Review weekly whether opt-ins are trending with traffic — a flat list with growing traffic means the capture surfaces are failing.
caveats: The source says growth specifics are 'a whole other video' — treat this as a list of levers to prioritize, not complete build instructions.
Keyword-based opt-in rules and required confirmation language vary by jurisdiction; verify compliance with your SMS platform and counsel.

cards.title: Write SMS campaigns that only say things worth interrupting for
cards.summary: SMS cannot afford to be vague: use clear, direct intents — sales, early access, restocks, back-in-stock, launches — because a 160-character message has no room for bland nurture content.
cards.use_when: Drafting the SMS slot in your campaign calendar, or reviewing a flat-performing SMS calendar that is heavy on general brand messaging.
steps: Cut broad, general and vague campaigns. In a short text there is not enough room to build curiosity, so a non-specific message fails to capture attention.
Anchor each campaign to a clear intention with an obvious click reason: sale, early access, restock/back-in-stock alert, new product launch.
Keep the message within the 160-character limit; going over splits the message into multiple parts and you are billed for more than one SMS.

Avoid MMS (image) messages unless the image is essential: the source notes images cost substantially more than a standard text. Compare marginal revenue against marginal send cost before defaulting to MMS.
Test SMS concepts against your email calendar — many campaigns are stronger as an email plus a spaced SMS reminder about the same event than as two independent messages.
caveats: 160-character single-message billing and MMS costing are platform/carrier-specific; confirm current pricing in your SMS provider.
The source's direct-intent list reflects its own accounts and does not rule out well-executed brand campaigns — it warns that vague content is the main failure mode.

cards.title: Set SMS sending frequency: one to two campaigns per week, never more
cards.summary: Keep SMS at about one campaign per week (two only for brands pushing over 8 figures annually), because frequency above that drives unsubscribes and annoyance faster than it adds revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many SMS campaign sends per week to schedule, or diagnosing an unsubscribe rate climbing above 1%.
steps: Start at roughly one SMS campaign per week. The source says this is the sweet spot it has personally found with clients.

If the brand is pushing over 8 figures annually, you may experiment with two campaigns per week. Anything more than two is likely overkill and produces higher unsubscribe rates with diminishing returns.
Set an unsubscribe-rate tripwire: above 1% means slow down your sending. Below 1% is normal; below 0.5% is excellent.

Adjust frequency by purchase cadence. Apparel can be bought roughly once a quarter, so more contact is tolerable; a furniture brand bought once every 18 months will not convert from a casual SMS, so pushing the same cadence will burn the list. Split test within your category.
Treat SMS as an intimate, personal channel: every send to a phone number is an intrusion, so only send when there is something concrete worth the interruption.
caveats: One to two per week is a source-specific heuristic from an agency's client base, not a calculated optimal derived from data; the source explicitly says to split test and that the number is industry-specific.
The 'over 8 figures annually' threshold is the presenter's rule of thumb.

cards.title: Build a calendar from retail events, not nurture filler
cards.summary: Plan SMS around fixed retail moments — back-in-stock, seasonal launches, gifting holidays, big sale weekends, VIP early access, product spotlights and flash sales — with big events getting multiple sends.
cards.use_when: Laying out next month's SMS campaign calendar for a fashion or seasonal ecommerce brand.
steps: Start with the fixed calendar: slot the big sale events first (the source's example uses Memorial Day, which got multiple sends rather than one).

Give major sales more than one send: e.g. a sale-start SMS on the Friday, an SMS on the actual holiday, and a VIP/subscriber early-access SMS on the Thursday before. Multiple sends on one event are a deliberate lever, not waste.
Add seasonal relevance: back-in-stock for returning items, introducing the season's collection, and a mid-season clearance send highlighting the sale section (source example: up to 50% off).
Layer gifting holidays that match the audience (e.g. Mother's Day for a women's fashion list).
Add a product-focus send spotlighting the hero product from the new collection, and an occasional one-day or weekend flash sale on a specific collection or few products.
Leave room for one brand/community-focused send with a call to action that is not purely transactional.
Keep the monthly count at one to two per week even when the calendar looks full, then split test whether raising frequency on a big event beats adding a new event.
caveats: The source populated about two SMS messages per week in its May example and immediately said your brand does not need to do that — it is an illustration, not a target.
Campaign-type effectiveness varies by category and purchase cycle; the source says to split test rather than copy the calendar.

cards.title: Send SMS during legal quiet hours and mirror your email
cards.summary: Do not send SMS before 8:00 a.m. or after 9:00 p.m.; aim for late morning to early afternoon and space SMS 5–6 hours after the matching email so the message reaches two devices.
cards.use_when: Choosing send times for SMS campaigns and pairing them with the day's email send.
steps: Respect legal quiet hours: avoid sending prior to 8:00 a.m. and after 9:00 p.m., because violating them can expose you to fines. The source's reasoning is also practical — waking someone with a text is the fastest way to get an unsubscribe.
Target the late morning to early afternoon window. The source's found sweet spot is roughly 11:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m., when people are on lunch or on a break.
Pair SMS with email as a reinforcement: if the email goes at 9:00 a.m., send the SMS follow-up later the same day, e.g. about 1:00 p.m. Space them 5 to 6 hours apart.
Use the pairing deliberately for launches and offers: the customer sees the email in the morning and the SMS in the afternoon, giving the same message a second chance on a second device.

If you enable quiet hours in the platform, remember it suppresses delivery during the restricted window rather than deferring sends to the next allowable time — plan your schedule so sends land inside the allowed window.
caveats: Quiet-hour windows and enforcement are jurisdiction-dependent; the 8 a.m.–9 p.m. band is the source's stated rule and should be verified against the TCPA or your local regulations.
The 11 a.m.–3 p.m. sweet spot is the source's anecdotal finding, and it says to test optimal send times for your list.

cards.title: Run SMS as a single-message omni-channel flow
cards.summary: Automated SMS flows are triggered by list signup, cart abandonment or product browse; most may legally contain only one SMS message (welcome is the exception with two), and they should run blended with email in one flow.
cards.use_when: Building the abandoned-cart, browse-abandonment and welcome automations for a store, or auditing whether existing SMS flows are compliant.
steps: Set up the three flows the source says drive the majority of revenue: welcome, abandoned cart, and browse abandonment.
Respect the one-message rule: for most flows you may only send a single SMS message, because additional messages are non-compliant. The abandoned-cart flow, for example, should have exactly one SMS.

Use the welcome-flow exception: you may have two SMS messages in the welcome flow. The source suggests the second goes out 2–3 days after the first, e.g. 'your 10% off is waiting' pointing to bestsellers.
Write the welcome message plainly: thank them for signing up, deliver the first-purchase discount code (source example: 10% off), and tell them to go shop.

Build the flows as omni-channel — SMS and email blended in the same automation — so email carries the longer content and SMS carries the short reminder. Klaviyo is preferred precisely because both appear under one flow.

Rely on the timing advantage: an abandoned cart SMS firing a couple of hours after the abandonment reaches the customer while intent is still high, and may reach someone who is on their phone but not checking email that day.
Plan for maintenance: the source says you get about 90% of the work done up front, then you split test, optimize and refresh periodically — do not literally set and forget.
Add a conversion incentive inside abandonment flows if margins allow; the source says customers receiving an extra incentive in the flow are more likely to convert.
caveats: The one-message-per-flow compliance rule and the two-message welcome exception are the source's stated understanding of SMS regulation; confirm current carrier and legal requirements before scaling.
The source cites a client generating over $100,000 per month from one SMS flow — a case study, not an expected result.
Extra abandonment incentives train customers to abandon; the source presents the tactic without addressing that risk.

cards.title: Measure SMS on clicks, unsubscribes and delivery — not open rates
cards.summary: Open rate is a vanity metric for SMS; target a 5–15% click rate, keep unsubscribe below 1% (excellent below 0.5%) and delivery above 90–95%.
cards.use_when: Reporting on SMS campaign performance, or setting up the dashboard and review cadence for the SMS channel.
steps: Ignore SMS open rates. The source calls them a vanity metric; click rate is the true read on engagement.
Target click rate of at least 5%, up to about 15%.
Keep unsubscribe rate below 1%; the source calls below 0.5% excellent. Above 1% means you are sending too much.
Keep delivery rate above 90% (good) and above 95% (excellent).

Diagnose and fix: for low click rates, tighten the engaged segment you send to and make the campaigns more direct. For high unsubscribe rates, send fewer messages, send to a more tightly engaged segment, and drop any informational/non-sales campaign. For low revenue per SMS, switch up the types of campaigns you send.

Review Cadence: check the platform about once a day for how the day's campaign is doing; weekly, review trends, line up the week's campaigns and inspect flows; monthly, compare performance to prior months and choose one or two structural changes (e.g. send two campaigns for the next big sale instead of one) to test.
caveats: During list growth, expect the unsubscribe rate to run higher simply because new subscribers are less engaged — the source notes this and does not treat early unsubscribes as a failure.
The 5–15% click and sub-1% unsubscribe bands are the source's recommended targets, not guaranteed results for every category.

cards.title: Avoid wasting budget through non-compliance and message-length errors
cards.summary: SMS law is stricter than email: never send to anyone who has not explicitly opted in, keep most flows to one message, avoid MMS costs, stay inside quiet hours and watch the 160-character limit.
cards.use_when: Auditing SMS list segments and send rules before a campaign, or onboarding a new SMS platform to reduce avoidable spend and legal risk.
steps: Segment only explicit SMS opt-ins. Unlike email, you cannot send SMS marketing to anyone who has not explicitly opted in — build the audience filter carefully and exclude ambiguous consent.
Keep most automated flows to one SMS message; the welcome flow is the only exception allowing two.
Enable quiet hours so no message is delivered before 8:00 a.m. or after 9:00 p.m.
Keep messages within 160 characters to avoid being billed for multiple message parts.
Default to standard SMS rather than MMS — images cost substantially more — and only choose MMS when the creative is essential to the offer.
Be aware of country-level credit costs (the source notes Canadian numbers may cost two credits versus one) when budgeting sends.
caveats: These rules are the source's stated compliance guidance and vary by jurisdiction and platform; verify with your SMS provider and legal counsel.
Explicit opt-in requirements mean purchased or scraped phone lists cannot be used for marketing.
